questions.stem: How does estrogen excretion change after the point marked menopause on this graph?
options: Falls immediately to zero
Declines toward a low plateau
Continues with large cyclic peaks
Rises steadily to its lifetime maximum
questions.explanation: The height of the curve at the menopausal transition and the slope after it tell different stories. The trace falls and then levels off above the baseline, consistent with continued nonfollicular estrogen production discussed in R4.
choice_rationales: Postmenopausal estrogen excretion stays above zero, even after the initial decline. This choice describes an abrupt loss of all estrogen production.
Postmenopausal estrogen excretion declines and then settles at a low plateau above zero. This choice describes the normal postmenopausal fall to a low plateau, which is what the figure shows.

The large cyclic estrogen peaks occur during the reproductive years. After menopause the curve settles at a low level without those repeated peaks. This choice describes persistence of cyclic ovarian estrogen peaks.
Estrogen excretion falls after menopause. The plotted lifetime peaks are earlier, during the reproductive years. This choice describes a rise in estrogen to its lifetime maximum.

questions.stem: If the central proton channel were more active, how would the use of the proton gradient change?

More gradient energy dissipates as heat with no direct ATP gain
The inner membrane stops allowing any proton return to the matrix
The gradient becomes steeper because proton leak falls sharply
choice_rationales: The central route bypasses ATP synthase. This choice describes increased ATP synthase flux.

The central UCP1 channel allows protons to cross without passing through ATP synthase. That uncoupling dissipates more of the gradient as heat. This choice describes uncoupling, in which proton leak dissipates energy as heat (as in brown fat thermogenesis), which is what the figure shows.

The drawn additional return path dissipates the gradient. This choice describes a steeper proton gradient from reduced leak.
questions.explanation: Nonshivering thermogenesis dissipates some of the stored proton gradient as heat. Because the leak bypasses ATP synthase, using more of this pathway does not produce more ATP per unit of gradient.
